title: The Atlas records MKR holders' informed consent so removing MKR's voting rights is not expropriation
content:
A.4.1.2.1 records that the Sky Protocol's technical infrastructure was upgraded to use SKY rather than MKR as its governance token. A.4.1.2.2.1 goes further: SKY "takes over all governance and economic rights previously held by MKR."

Stripping an existing token of every right it had is the kind of act that invites a legitimacy challenge, and A.4.1.2.1.1 is written specifically to foreclose one. It states in bold that "MKR holders have voted to approve the deprecation of MKR as the governance token of the Sky Protocol **with full knowledge of the changes being proposed**," links the exact poll, and then enumerates what the approval covers: "including, but not limited to, the removal of voting rights from MKR and the Delayed Upgrade Penalty."

Three moves make this more than a citation. It names the consenting class (MKR holders, i.e. the people harmed). It asserts *informed* consent, not merely a passing vote. And it pre-commits that the penalty — a cost imposed on holders who fail to act — was inside the scope of what was approved, which is exactly the clause a late converter would otherwise dispute.

The general lesson: where a governance system removes rights from its own prior stakeholders, the durable defence is a recorded, scoped, pre-action consent artifact. The Atlas treats that record as a permanent part of the ruleset, not as historical trivia.
description: A.4.1.2.1.1 cites the specific poll and asserts full knowledge of the consequences, including loss of voting rights and the Delayed Upgrade Penalty — consent captured before the fact, in bold.
